chunks: Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:
"From stagnant altered water, he may perform wudu (ablution) with it unless he finds other water besides it."

This is when the water has become altered on its own; then there is no objection to using it. But if some impurity has entered it and altered it, then its use is absolutely not permissible in any way, according to what we have already stated. Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: If something from the impurities falls into still water, and it is kurr—its amount being one thousand two hundred Baghdadi ratls or more—then nothing renders it impure unless it changes because of it, as we mentioned regarding flowing waters. This is when the water is in a pond or a well-like pit. But if it is in a well, cistern, or vessel, then it is corrupted by whatever dies in it from creatures with flowing blood, and by all impurities that come into contact with it; and purification with it is not permissible until it is purified. If the water in ponds and pits is less than one thousand two hundred ratls, it takes the ruling of well-water and basin-water that are corrupted by whatever impurity falls into them, and purification with it is not permissible. We have already explained what indicates the limit of kurr, and that whenever water reaches kurr or exceeds it, it does not bear impurity except that which changes its color or taste. And we explained that whatever is less than kurr is rendered impure by whatever impurity enters it, even if it does not alter its color or taste. As for the ruling of wells, we shall mention it later, if Allah Most High wills. Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: Purification with mixed waters is not permissible, such as bean-water, saffron-water, rose-water, myrtle-water, ushnaan-water, and the like, until the water is pure and free of what overcomes it, even if it is pure in itself and not impurifying to what it meets. The proof for that is what we have already presented from the verse, and that Allah Most High has allowed us purification with that to which the unqualified name of water applies. So if these waters are not called water except with qualification, then wudu (ablution) with them must not be permissible. Also indicating this is that wudu (ablution) is a legal ruling, and that by which one performs wudu (ablution) is also a legal ruling; and what the law decisively established for performing wudu (ablution) is that to which the unqualified name of water applies. Thus, what is other than that must not suffice for wudu (ablution), because there is no proof for it. Also indicating that is the report we have already mentioned from the statement of Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, when he was asked: A man has milk with him—may he perform wudu (ablution) with it for salat (prayer)? He said: "No. It is only water and earth." We have already explained earlier that there is no difference between someone saying, "I only have such-and-such for you with me," and his saying, "I have nothing for you except such-and-such," in that in both cases it indicates that whatever is besides what is mentioned after innamā is negated. So it is as though he said: It is not permissible to perform wudu (ablution) except with water and earth. And these mixed waters are not among what the unqualified name of water applies to, so their legal validity must be negated.

As for the report narrated by Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man performs ghusl with rose-water and performs wudu (ablution) with it for salat (prayer)? He said: "There is no objection to that." This report is anomalous, extremely anomalous, even if it is repeated in the books and source-texts, for its basis is only Yūnus from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, and no one else narrated it. The group has unanimously agreed to abandon acting upon its apparent meaning, and that whose ruling is such is not acted upon. Even if it were sound, it is possible that what was intended by it was wuḍūʾ in the sense of beautification, and we have already explained earlier that this is called wuḍūʾ. No one may say that the report states he asked him about rose-water, whether he may perform wudu (ablution) with it for salat (prayer), because that does not conflict with what we have said; for it is possible that he uses it for beautification while at the same time intending by it to enter into salat (prayer), since whenever he uses a pleasant fragrance for entering into salat (prayer) and for intimate discourse with his Lord, that is better than intending mere enjoyment by it apart from seeking the Face of Allah Most High. In this is the invalidation of what the questioner assumed. It is also possible that what he عليه السلام intended by his saying 'rose-water' was water into which roses had fallen, for that may be called rose-water even if it is not extracted from it, because everything that is adjacent to something else acquires from it the name of attribution to it, even when adjacency is what is intended. Do you not see that they say: jar-water, factory-water, and waterskin-water, even though these attributions are only attributions of adjacency and nothing else? In this is the invalidation of what they assumed.

key_terms.الصَّعِيدُ: earth used for tayammum when water cannot be used
key_terms.النَّجَاسَةِ: ritual impurity that can contaminate water
key_terms.الْمَاءِ الْآجِنِ: water whose condition has changed naturally through stagnation
key_terms.الْمِيَاهِ الْمُضَافَةِ: mixed or qualified waters to which the unqualified term water does not apply
key_terms.شَاذٌّ: an anomalous report not relied upon in legal practice
key_terms.كُرًّا: the threshold quantity of water that is not rendered impure unless changed

ai.seo_question: Can wudu (ablution) be performed with stagnant water or mixed waters like rose-water in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the fiqh of taharah and the legal distinctions between naturally altered water, impure water, kurr water, and mixed waters used for wudu (ablution). It also addresses an anomalous hadith about rose-water and explains why it is not acted upon in deriving the legal ruling.
